The BFA in Film/Media is an intensive, experiential degree that integrates advanced creative practice with critical and historical study.
The curriculum emphasizes sequential training in film and media production alongside rigorous engagement with theory, research, and analysis.
Students develop technical and conceptual proficiency through sustained coursework, collaborative projects, and advanced culminating work that reflects professional standards and disciplined artistic inquiry.
FLM 496 (Capstone Seminar in Film/Media) and FLM 397 (1 Credit) BFA portfolio are required in the junior year; and FLM 497 (BFA Capstone) is required in the senior year.
Students learn to work with the evolving and overlapping technologies involved in the production of moving images.

A wide range of courses is available to the Film/Media student-courses that examine the historical, theoretical, and global approaches to the analysis and creation of moving images.
The Film/Media program prepares students for careers in such areas as independent filmmaking; animation and media design; film and television industries, advertising, marketing, public relations, and media criticism.
Graduates of this program are also prepared to continue with graduate studies in film and media production for an M.F.A.
Students majoring in the Film BFA must complete a minimum of 52 credits (maximum 67) in approved courses toward the major.

Because the study and practice of food systems intersects with a wide range of other disciplines, the major is also ideal for those who wish to combine interdisciplinary training in food systems with a complementary major.
Students completing the program will graduate with the skills and knowledge needed to contribute to the development of sustainable, equitable, and resilient food systems from local to global scales.
The major allows participants to explore diverse aspects of the food supply chain from production to processing/distribution to consumption to waste management and recovery, with an emphasis on systems thinking, food system policy, and social, cultural, and political context.

By the time of degree completion, students will be uniquely positioned to enter the workforce in the growing field of sustainable food systems or to pursue opportunities in graduate education or research addressing the challenges of securing access to safe and affordable food for a growing population.
SFS BA students will pursue a curriculum offering breadth across the natural and social sciences and the arts and humanities.

A robust capstone experience in which students master the ability to address the complex challenges in the area of sustainable food systems through experiential learning in interdisciplinary teams.
Students are required to take a total of six credits, including three credits of internship or special project and an additional three credits in another capstone course.

Compared to the BS in SFS, the BA allows students greater flexibility in selecting courses relevant to their specific interests.

The BFA in Film/Media is an intensive, experiential degree that integrates advanced creative practice with critical and historical study.
The curriculum emphasizes sequential training in film and media production alongside rigorous engagement with theory, research, and analysis.

Students learn to work with the evolving and overlapping technologies involved in the production of moving images.

A wide range of courses is available to the Film/Media student-courses that examine the historical, theoretical, and global approaches to the analysis and creation of moving images.
The Film/Media program prepares students for careers in such areas as independent filmmaking; animation and media design; film and television industries, advertising, marketing, public relations, and media criticism.
Graduates of this program are also prepared to continue with graduate studies in film and media production for an M.F.A.

Students in the program demonstrate strong interest in advanced media production, and an evaluation of the current population indicates that approximately 25% of our annual graduates would pursue a BFA in film/media if available.
This reflects a clear demand for a rigorous, production-focused degree within Rhode Island, where no large public university currently offers such a pathway.
Regional competition includes private institutions like RISD, which emphasizes artistic and experimental film, and Emerson College in Boston, which offers a highly regarded, production-intensive BFA in media arts.
A public BFA program in Rhode Island would provide accessible, hands-on professional training, prepare graduates for careers in the growing media industry, and retain local talent that might otherwise leave the state for comparable programs.
